title: Optimizers
oneLiner: An optimiser is the rule for turning gradients into weight changes; smarter rules add momentum, give each weight its own step size, and change the step size over time.

what.html:
An optimiser decides how to move the weights after each batch. Plain gradient descent steps straight downhill by a fixed amount. Better optimisers remember past steps (momentum), scale each weight's step by how bumpy its history has been (adaptive methods like RMSprop and Adam), and shrink the step size as training goes on (schedules).

Everyday versionWalking down a long, narrow, steep-sided valley in fog. Taking equal steps straight downhill makes you zigzag between the walls. Momentum is like building up speed along the valley floor; adaptive methods are like taking short steps across the steep sides and long steps along the gentle slope.

why.html:
• Networks have millions of weights and no formula for the best ones: we can only take steps.
  • Loss surfaces have narrow valleys, flat plateaus and saddle points where plain gradient descent zigzags or stalls.
  • Different weights need different step sizes; one global learning rate is a compromise.
  • The optimiser and learning rate often decide whether training works at all.

how.title: One gradient step
how.html: On the bowl f = x² + y² starting at (3, 4), the gradient is (6, 8). With step size 0.1 we move to (2.4, 3.2) and the loss drops from 25 to 16. For every common loss, the gradient boils down to "prediction minus target", which keeps backpropagation simple.

how.title: What makes optimisation hard
how.html: Saddle points: flat in some directions, downhill in others. Plateaus: almost no slope, so progress crawls. Many valleys: different starting points end in different places. Signs you're stuck: the loss curve flattens while validation error is still high, and gradients shrink towards zero.

how.title: All data, one example, or a mini-batch
how.html: Batch gradient descent uses every example per step (accurate, slow). SGD uses one (fast, noisy). Mini-batches of 32–256 are the practical middle: with 10,000 examples and batches of 32 you take 313 steps per pass.

how.title: The long narrow valley
how.html: The slides' test problem, w₁² + 4w₂², is 4× steeper in one direction. With step size 0.1, w₂ is solved almost at once while w₁ creeps along. Too big a step and it bounces or explodes; too small and it barely moves.

how.title: Momentum: build up speed
how.html: Keep a running "velocity": 90% of the last velocity plus the new gradient, and move along it. Consistent directions speed up, zigzags cancel out. Because it amplifies steps, momentum needs a smaller learning rate. Nesterov peeks ahead along the velocity before measuring the slope, so it brakes earlier.

how.title: Adaptive step sizes: AdaGrad and RMSprop
how.html: Divide each weight's step by the size of its recent gradients: steep directions get small steps, gentle directions larger ones. AdaGrad adds up all past squared gradients, so its steps eventually shrink to nothing. RMSprop uses a fading average instead, so it keeps learning. In the slides' example, w₂'s effective rate becomes half of w₁'s automatically.

how.title: Adam: momentum + adaptive steps
how.html: Adam keeps two running averages: of the gradients (like momentum) and of the squared gradients (like RMSprop), with a correction for starting at zero. Each weight moves about one learning-rate's worth per step in a sensible direction, which makes Adam forgiving. It's the default choice; AdamW applies weight decay separately and is standard for Transformers.

how.title: Change the learning rate over time
how.html: Take big steps early, small careful ones late. Step decay divides the rate by 10 every 30 epochs; exponential shrinks it smoothly; cosine glides from high to low along a half-wave. Warmup starts from zero and ramps up over the first few epochs so a freshly initialised model isn't knocked off balance.

how.title: Gradient clipping
how.html: Occasionally a gradient is enormous and one step wrecks the model (NaNs, spikes). Clipping caps it: by norm shrinks the whole gradient to length τ and keeps its direction (the usual choice); by value caps each component separately, which can tilt the direction. Essential for RNNs and Transformers.

how.title: Batch size, debugging and when to stop
how.html: Bigger batches give smoother gradients but fewer steps; if you double the batch, roughly double the learning rate and add warmup. Debug from the loss curve: not falling → rate too small; bouncing → divide by 10; exploding → clip. Stop with early stopping: when validation loss hasn't improved for "patience" epochs, stop and restore the best checkpoint.

how.title: Choosing and tuning
how.html: New project: Adam with learning rate 0.001. Tuned production vision model: SGD + momentum with a schedule. RNNs: RMSprop; sparse features: AdaGrad. Tune the learning rate first, then batch size, then the schedule; leave the other settings at their defaults. Always overfit a tiny batch first as a sanity check.

demo.html: Press Step three times and compare with the slides' tables: GD reaches loss ≈4.20, momentum ≈8.44 (it overshoots in w₂), RMSprop ≈24.01 and Adam ≈28.52 (the slides' rounded tables show 4.21, 8.43, 23.93, 28.51), the last two taking small even steps. Then press Play and watch which ones win over 100 steps, and try the learning-rate multiplier.

example.html:
The narrow valley w₁² + 4w₂² run through every optimiser. Schedules: 0.1 → 0.01 at epoch 30 (step); 0.061 at epoch 10 (exponential); warmup to 0.1 over 5 epochs then cosine to 0.001. Early stopping: best model at epoch 35, stop at 60, restore 35.

Supplementary A network-traffic forecaster trained with Adam suddenly spikes to NaN during a holiday-traffic batch; adding norm clipping at 1.0 and a short warmup fixes it without slowing normal training.

misunderstandings: It's a robust default, but tuned SGD + momentum often generalises better (especially in vision), and on simple problems plain GD can win.
Momentum lets you keep the same learning rate.
It amplifies steps (about 10× for β = 0.9), so it usually needs a smaller rate.
Weight decay in Adam is the same as L2 regularisation.
With adaptive optimisers they differ; AdamW applies decay separately.
It only limits very large gradients.
Bigger batches are just faster with no downside.
Fewer updates per epoch; they need learning-rate scaling and warmup and can generalise worse.
takeaways: Mini-batch gradient descent: θ ← θ − η·g; the learning rate is the most important setting.
Momentum (v ← βv + g) speeds up consistent directions and damps zigzags; Nesterov looks ahead.
AdaGrad/RMSprop scale each weight's step by its gradient history; Adam combines this with momentum and bias correction; AdamW decouples weight decay.
Schedules (step, exponential, cosine) plus warmup; clip gradients by norm for stability.
Monitor train/validation curves, use early stopping, start with Adam η = 0.001, tune LR → batch → schedule.
thirty: An optimiser turns gradients into parameter updates. Mini-batch gradient descent steps against the average gradient of a batch, but one learning rate for every weight zigzags in narrow valleys. Momentum keeps a velocity, ninety percent of the previous one plus the new gradient, which speeds up consistent directions; Nesterov evaluates the gradient after a look-ahead. AdaGrad and RMSprop divide each weight's step by the root of its accumulated or averaged squared gradients, so steep directions take smaller steps. Adam combines momentum and RMSprop with bias correction and is the default, with AdamW decoupling weight decay. In practice we add warmup and a decay schedule such as cosine, clip gradients by norm, watch training and validation curves, and use early stopping. Tune the learning rate first.

check.q: GD on f = x² + y² from (3, 4) with η = 0.1 moves to…

opts: Keeps 90% of the previous velocity and adds the new gradient

check.q: Why does AdaGrad eventually stop learning?
opts: Its sum of squared gradients keeps growing, shrinking the step to zero
